clue.text: War-dance celebrating such a costly victory?

definitions.meaning: an ancient Greek dance performed in armour
a win gained at ruinous cost, named after King Pyrrhus of Epirus

explanation.surface: Troops dance in celebration of a win that cost them dearly.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the armoured dance of ancient Greece and a triumph so expensive it amounts to defeat.

clue.text: Old documents here? Pay state for keeping quiet

indicators.note: the outer letters keep the other piece inside them

parts.note: taken as written
p, piano, is the musical direction for quiet
RI is Rhode Island, a US state

explanation.surface: A request for state money to buy someone's silence.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient writings on reed paper are the old documents meant; 'here' points to the material on which they survive.

clue.text: Train soldiers, upsetting section on exercise at first

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers

indicators.note: in a down clue, upsetting turns the word section's synonym upside down, reading it backwards

parts.note: a unit is a section

indicators.note: the opening letter of exercise is used

explanation.surface: Soldiers train while a unit is thrown into disarray by the start of drill.
explanation.definitionFit: A train is a body of followers or attendants accompanying an important person.

clue.text: Restraints observed by workers outside buffet

indicators.note: the workers' letters go round the other piece

parts.note: hands are workers
to cuff is to buffet or strike

explanation.surface: Workers outside a buffet bar keep an eye on the bars that restrain.
explanation.definitionFit: Linked metal rings locked round the wrists restrain prisoners.

clue.text: Far-seeing carnival toy-maker

indicators.note: a maker makes something new from material, so the letters of carnival toy are refashioned

explanation.surface: A toy-maker at the fair is commended for vision.
explanation.definitionFit: A person with second sight perceives things beyond normal vision, so is far-seeing.

clue.text: Saw bishop about voting system? Quite the opposite

indicators.note: the clue's order puts bishop before the rest; this phrase tells us to place the bishop last instead

parts.note: PR is proportional representation, a voting system
over can mean concerning or about
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A bishop holds forth on electoral reform, or perhaps the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the clue gives B + OVER + PR; 'Quite the opposite' flips the order to PR + OVER + B.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying or maxim, a synonym of a traditional pithy saying.

clue.text: Bird food

definitions.meaning: the magpie, called a ... in old usage
a pastry dish with a filling

explanation.definitionFit: Pie is an old name for the magpie and also a baked pastry dish.

clue.text: Public turned up to put priest inside

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means reading bottom to top, so the letters run backwards
with inside, put signals placing the priest within the other word
with put, inside signals the priest goes within the other word

parts.note: taken as written
Rev is short for Reverend, a priest

explanation.surface: Something public turned up for placing a priest within.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put' and 'inside' build TREVO, which 'turned up' then reads upwards in this down light; 'Public' looks like a noun but means open, done in view.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done openly, in full view, is out in the open and not hidden.

clue.text: Having read out letter, dine out in Ankara, mister

indicators.note: the letter is spoken as its name, so we write how it sounds

parts.note: F is a letter of the alphabet

indicators.note: out signals the word dine is rearranged

explanation.surface: Having read a letter aloud, someone in Ankara goes out to dine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'read out' spells the letter F as EFF; 'out' scrambles DINE into ENDI.
explanation.definitionFit: A Turkish title of respect, used as a courtesy form of address for a man, like sir.

clue.text: Gang-girl's neckerchief

parts.note: a band is a gang
Anna is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A gang member's girlfriend wears a scarf round her neck.
explanation.definitionFit: A brightly coloured spotted scarf worn round the neck or head is a kind of neckerchief.

clue.text: Wine swallowed by river goddess — one of great power

indicators.note: being swallowed means going inside, so the wine sits within the other pieces

parts.note: the Po is the great river of northern Italy
Ate is the Greek goddess of mischief and ruin
tent is a deep-red Spanish wine

explanation.surface: A river goddess gulps down wine, showing herself a mighty being.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallowed by' needs the wine within both river and goddess, so the two outer pieces join around it; tent as a wine is an old crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch or ruler with absolute authority is someone wielding immense might.

clue.text: Like a little creature helping Weasel find the answer

indicators.note: a helping is a portion, so a portion of the words Weasel find is served up here

explanation.surface: A small animal assists a weasel in finding the solution.
explanation.definitionFit: Elves are tiny mythical beings, so something resembling one is small and sprite-like.

clue.text: Police force covering Northern Ireland, comprising strange -old characters

indicators.note: the police force wraps round the other piece, so its letters go outside

parts.note: RUC is the Royal Ulster Constabulary, the former Northern Ireland police force

explanation.surface: The Ulster police patrol a province full of odd old-timers.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient Germanic alphabets used mysterious letter-forms, so text in that script is made of strange antique letters.

clue.text: Turin air, a change from Hope's territory

indicators.note: a change of letters signals they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Italian air in Turin offers a break from the place one hoped for.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Hope set The Prisoner of Zenda in an imaginary Central European kingdom; 'Hope' looks like a feeling but is the author.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Hope invented this fictional Balkan-style kingdom as the setting of his adventure novels.

clue.text: True case it's ridiculous to revive

indicators.note: something ridiculous is absurd and disordered, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: It's absurd to bring a true case back to life.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring someone back to consciousness or life is to restore them.

clue.text: Composure of the number one owner

definitions.meaning: number one is oneself, so this is ownership held by oneself

explanation.surface: Calmness belonging to the chief proprietor.
explanation.definitionFit: Being master of one's own feelings is calmness; and literally it is ownership in which 'number one', oneself, is the holder.

clue.text: Lear's body was perfectly so

parts.note: points to Edward Lear's nonsense verse, where a character's body has a round ball shape, not to King Lear

explanation.surface: A remark on King Lear's flawless physique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lear' suggests Shakespeare's king; it is the nonsense poet Edward Lear.
explanation.definitionFit: The shape described is round like a globe, the form Edward Lear gives a character's body.

clue.text: Listening instrument to put in circular room

indicators.note: the word to is placed within the other pieces

parts.note: O is circular in shape
scope means room or space to act
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hearing device is installed in a round room.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor's instrument for looking into the ear is used in examining hearing.

clue.text: Dependant of Chesterton's man with a great distance to travel?

definitions.text: with a great distance to travel?

indicators.note: of means belonging to, so the dependant is placed after the man it belongs to

parts.note: G K Chesterton wrote The Man Who Was Thursday
a child is a dependant

explanation.surface: The offspring of a Chesterton hero faces a long journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme 'Monday's child' says this child 'has far to go', which the definition echoes.
explanation.definitionFit: In the traditional rhyme about birth days, the one born on that weekday has far to go.

clue.text: Defenceless, with two members absent

definitions.meaning: members are limbs, so this means with no arms

explanation.definitionFit: Having no weapons leaves one defenceless; read literally it means lacking both arms, two limbs.

clue.text: Formerly hindering 22's business

definitions.meaning: let once meant hinder, as in 'without let or hindrance'
22-down is one who rents property out, whose trade is renting

explanation.definitionFit: The archaic verb let means to obstruct; and renting out property is the trade of the person in 22.

clue.text: Stupid person, he, to invest!

parts.note: a clot is a stupid person
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fool, he, is told to put his money in!
explanation.walkthrough: 'invest' looks financial, but here means robe or dress, as in investiture.
explanation.definitionFit: To invest someone is to dress them in robes of office, so to dress.

clue.text: Past eight, perhaps, when this is cooked?

definitions.text: Past eight, perhaps, when this is cooked?

indicators.note: cooking mixes ingredients, so the letters of Past eight are mixed up

explanation.surface: A late supper of pasta, ready some time after eight o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: cook the letters and you get the pasta itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Long thin pasta strands are what is cooked here, and the scrambled letters produce them.

clue.text: The French yesterday accepted the Queen's letter

indicators.note: the French word takes in the other piece

parts.note: hier is French for yesterday
R is for Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: Yesterday the French took delivery of the Queen's letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letter' is not mail but one who lets, a renter.
explanation.definitionFit: One who lets out property, or who rents things, can be called a letter.

clue.text: A rodent — the Spanish honey-badger

parts.note: a rat is a rodent
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: A rodent is compared to a Spanish honey-badger.
explanation.definitionFit: This African and Asian mammal of the weasel family is commonly called the honey-badger.

clue.text: Kipling's lyre-smiting poet eating the right seafood?

indicators.note: the poet takes in the other piece, so its letter goes inside

parts.note: Kipling wrote "When 'Omer smote 'is bloomin' lyre", dropping the H of Homer
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A lyre-playing poet from Kipling dines on the proper seafood.
explanation.definitionFit: A Channel Islands shellfish, also called an abalone, is eaten as a delicacy.

clue.text: He will accept nothing, as a rule

definitions.text: He will accept nothing, as a rule

parts.words: He will accept nothing, as a rule
parts.note: read as 'he will accept no rule', the clue describes someone who rejects all government and authority

explanation.surface: A man who usually turns everything down.
explanation.definitionFit: A believer in abolishing government acknowledges no ruling power at all.

clue.text: Tool unknown in a European capital

indicators.note: in means the unknown goes within the other letters
the capital, or initial, letter of European is taken

parts.note: x is the classic algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A tool never heard of in some European capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'European capital' suggests a city; it is the initial letter E.
explanation.definitionFit: A chopping implement with a heavy blade on a handle is a woodworking tool.

clue.text: Finish not so good without wife to approve

parts.note: end means finish

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the wife's letter is dropped

parts.note: worse means not so good

explanation.surface: A man ends up worse off without his wife's approval.
explanation.definitionFit: To back or sanction something formally is to give it one's support.

clue.text: Poem provides egghead with hint about biblical king

parts.note: the head of egg is its first letter, E

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the hint goes round the king

parts.note: a clue is a hint
Og was the giant king of Bashan in the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A clever person offers a poem with a pointer about a king of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastoral verse, such as Virgil's, is a short poem in dialogue form.
